title: Screen PPI, DPI and Retina: The Pixel-Density Math That Matters
h1: Screen PPI vs DPI — pixel density, viewing distance and 'Retina'
description: PPI = √(w² + h²) / diagonal-in-inches. A 27" 4K panel is 163 PPI, a 15.6" 1080p laptop is 141 PPI. Here is when density stops mattering.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against VESA DisplayHDR specs, Apple HIG (Retina), ISO 12233:2023 (resolution measurement) and Snellen visual-acuity limits

hero: A 27-inch 4K monitor is 163 PPI. A 15.6-inch 1080p laptop is 141 PPI. An iPhone 15 Pro is 460 PPI. The eye can resolve about 60 PPI per degree of view — beyond that, more pixels are wasted photons.
body: PPI (pixels per inch) and DPI (dots per inch) are numerically identical for displays; the terms diverged in the print world, where DPI counts ink drops and PPI counts image pixels. For a rectangular panel, PPI is the diagonal pixel count divided by the diagonal in inches. The full formula: PPI = √(width_px² + height_px²) / diagonal_inches. Manufacturers quote diagonal because that's how TVs have been sold since 1927 (RCA TT-5).
## The exact formula

> PPI = √(w_px² + h_px²) / d_in
> Dot pitch (mm) = 25.4 / PPI
> Human acuity limit: 60 cycles/degree = 1 arc-minute (Snellen 20/20)
> Retina threshold: PPI × viewing_distance_in ≥ 3438  (Apple's rule: 1 pixel < 1 arc-min at typical distance)
## Common panels at a glance
## The 'Retina' threshold

Apple's marketing claim: at typical viewing distance, one pixel subtends less than 1 arc-minute — the Snellen 20/20 resolving limit. Math: 1 arc-min = 1/60° = tan⁻¹(pixel_pitch / viewing_distance). Rearranging: PPI × distance_in ≥ 3438. Phone at 12" → needs 287 PPI. Laptop at 20" → needs 172 PPI. 27" monitor at 24" → needs 143 PPI. TV at 108" (9 ft) → needs 32 PPI (which is why 1080p looks fine on a 65" from the couch).
## Worked example — is 4K wasted on a 24" monitor?

24" 4K = 184 PPI. Typical monitor distance 20" (arm's length). Required Retina PPI = 3438/20 = 172. Verdict: 184 > 172, so pixels are *just* below arc-minute resolution — you gain crispness in text but the returns are diminishing. At 32" from the screen (leaned back), required drops to 107 PPI, so 1440p (122 PPI) is already Retina-level. This is why productivity users prefer 27" 4K (163 PPI, cleaner text scaling at 150%) over 24" 4K.
## Print DPI is a different animal

Print DPI counts ink dots, and each pixel needs 4–16 dots to reproduce colour via halftoning or error diffusion. Rule of thumb: image PPI should be 300 for print quality at reading distance; printers output 600–2400 DPI to render that. A 300-PPI 8×10 photo is 2400×3000 pixels = 7.2 MP — the reason 8 MP cameras were the 2005 sweet spot for consumer photo prints.
## Viewing distance rules of thumb

| Content | Optimal distance | Required PPI |
|---|---|---|
| Phone (email/reading) | 10–14" | 245–345 |
| Tablet | 15–18" | 190–230 |
| Laptop | 18–24" | 143–190 |
| Desktop monitor | 20–30" | 115–172 |
| Living-room TV | 6–10 ft | 29–48 |
| Cinema screen | 20–40 ft | 7–14 |
| VR headset (per eye) | ~1.5" effective | 2300+ (arc-min at wide FOV) |
## Sub-pixel geometry

PPI is one dimension of sharpness; sub-pixel layout is another. Standard RGB stripe (LCD, most OLEDs) gives full luminance resolution per pixel. Samsung PenTile diamond OLED shares green sub-pixels — effective resolution is ~82% of the marketed count (Soneira, DisplayMate 2013). This is why 460 PPI on an iPhone (LTPO OLED, RGB) reads sharper than 500 PPI on some older PenTile Androids.
## Scaling and the '1.5×' curse

Windows scales UI by 100/125/150/175/200%; macOS uses integer 2× 'HiDPI' + a rendered downsample. Non-integer scaling (150%) forces sub-pixel rounding — 1px CSS borders become 1.5px, get rounded to 1 or 2, producing visible thickness variation. A 3840×2160 27" at 150% shows fewer artefacts than a 3200×1800 27" at 150% because the base grid is denser. If you buy a laptop for text work, prefer a PPI that lands cleanly at 200% scaling: 15.6" 1080p (141 PPI, 100%) or 14" 3024×1964 (254 PPI, 200%).
## Angular resolution is what your eye cares about

60 PPI/degree is the healthy 20/20 limit; 20/10 acuity (rare) doubles it. VR headsets aim for 60 PPD (pixels per degree) with 100°+ FOV — hence the 3386 PPI in Vision Pro. Compared with a 27" 4K monitor at 24" distance covering ~60° of vision (with head-turn), the monitor delivers ~64 PPD — right at the Retina limit. Any 5K/8K push on desktop delivers negligible perceived improvement; the money is better spent on colour gamut (DCI-P3, Rec.2020) or refresh rate.
## The five-second recap
PPI = √(w²+h²)/diagonal. Retina threshold ≈ 3438 / viewing_distance_in. Beyond ~60 PPD there is no perceivable gain. 4K helps text scaling more than image sharpness.

faqs.q: PPI vs DPI — which term is right for my monitor?
faqs.a: For displays, use PPI. DPI is a print term meaning ink drops per inch. Windows still labels its scaling slider 'DPI' for historical Win95 reasons, but the value shown (96 default) is actually a PPI reference.

Only up to your eye's resolving power at the intended distance. Beyond ~60 PPD, extra pixels burn GPU, battery and money for no visible benefit — except in VR where wide FOV keeps hunger for pixels high.

faqs.q: Why do 4K TVs look worse than 4K monitors up close?
faqs.a: TVs use aggressive image processing (motion smoothing, upscaling) tuned for 3 m viewing. Their sub-pixel layout, bit-depth and text rendering optimize for video, not thin fonts. A 40" 4K TV as a monitor at 60 cm is 110 PPI — sharp on paper, muddy in practice.

faqs.q: What PPI does my phone need?
faqs.a: 300+ for comfortable reading at 12" distance; 400+ for AR-quality overlays. Beyond 500 PPI on a handheld device, gains are measurable in labs but not visible to typical users (source: Soneira DisplayMate 2015 shootouts).

faqs.q: How do I calculate dot pitch?
faqs.a: Dot pitch (mm between adjacent pixel centres) = 25.4 / PPI. A 92 PPI 1080p 24" monitor has 0.276 mm dot pitch — the CRT-era 'good enough' standard set by NEC in 1998.
